title: US Treasury bought yen in July, its first intervention since 1998, as yen nears 160 again
body: The report confirms that the US is a willing partner in yen support, not just a bystander. That raises the risk for anyone betting heavily on dollar-yen above 160, a level that now looks well defended. Positioning is likely to turn more cautious as the pair approaches the summer's intervention zone, and volatility could spike on any further rate checks. Rate expectations still favour the dollar, though, because the US economy is resilient and inflation is high. That means intervention may only slow the yen's slide unless the BOJ follows through with a December hike to 1.5%. --- Yesterday: Japan's Mimura warns yen moves are too rapid as USD/JPY pushes back toward 160 --- Washington has now confirmed that it put its own money behind the yen this summer. With the currency back near 160, the main question is whether Tokyo and Washington can hold that line again.

title: BlackRock sees gold support intact despite near 30% drop from record, expects milder gains
body: BlackRock's view backs the idea that gold's correction has been driven by rates, not by fading long-term demand. Near-term direction depends mainly on real yields and the dollar. With markets pricing further Fed tightening, rallies are likely to be hard to sustain, and gold has tended to fall rather than rise as geopolitical risk lifts oil, inflation and hike expectations. Central bank buying offers some support on dips, but BlackRock expects that buying to slow from its recent pace. Silver remains the more cyclical and riskier of the two, more exposed to swings in industrial demand and growth expectations. --- Earlier Three drivers setting gold's tone as December Fed hike bets build, according to Standard Chartered --- BlackRock says gold's structural support from central banks is intact, but with real yields and the dollar working against it, investors should expect it to stabilise portfolios rather than repeat last year's surge.

title: UBS sees no RBA cuts until late 2027 as AI boom fuels inflation, growth slowing to 1.4%
body: UBS's view is more hawkish than current market pricing, which has moved towards RBA cuts within months. That leaves front-end Australian bond yields exposed if upcoming inflation data run hot. For the Australian dollar, a longer restrictive period would support rate differentials, but the weak domestic growth outlook limits how much it can benefit. The February RBA meeting is now a live risk if quarterly core inflation stays near a 1% pace. UBS's upbeat global outlook depends partly on a Middle East resolution bringing oil prices down, so a lasting oil shock would hurt both growth and the inflation outlook. --- UBS says the AI boom is giving Australia the inflation now and the productivity later, which means no RBA cuts until late 2027 and a private sector that will feel like it's in recession.

title: Anthropic IPO targets around $1 trillion valuation, half the $2 trillion once whispered
body: A listing of this size will test how much appetite there is for AI risk after the recent tech selloff. Strong demand would suggest investors still see value in leading AI names at lower valuations. The roughly $87bn raised between the public offering and the strategic placement could pull money away from other tech holdings in the run-up to pricing. Strategic investors Nvidia, Micron, Alphabet and Microsoft are also tied to the deal, so a strong debut could support the wider AI infrastructure trade. A weak one would likely weigh on it. - Earlier: Anthropic reserves up to 20% of its $64 billion IPO for retail investors Anthropic IPO oversubscribed several times ahead of record $90 billion listing - Anthropic is coming to market at about half the valuation once talked about, with very fast growth and a large cash pile, but also with compute commitments that will test whether that growth can last.

title: Goldman sees AI spending hitting $1.4 trillion by end-2027, nearly 4% of the US economy
body: Goldman's forecast supports the AI infrastructure trade, especially chipmakers, chip equipment makers and networking suppliers, which get the most from a spending path well above consensus. Its point that most AI hardware is imported matters for macro traders. Strong capex does not mean equally strong US GDP growth, and the gap shows up instead in a wider trade deficit and in demand for Asian supply chains. Downplaying the regulatory risk from the midterms may ease one worry that has weighed on data centre-linked stocks. Funding costs remain the main pressure point, as Fed hike expectations push borrowing costs higher. --- Earlier: Cerebras raises 2026 outlook, sees revenue tripling in 2027 as $26bn backlog builds Applied Materials beats on Q4 and guides above forecasts as chip equipment demand holds Cisco beats and lifts FY27 view as AI revenue from hyperscalers set to more than double --- Goldman expects AI spending to reach a $1.4 trillion annual pace by the end of 2027 and keep driving US capex, but because much of the hardware is imported, the direct boost to US GDP is far smaller than the spending total.

title: Oil Holds Advance as Trump Downplays Iran Deal

title: Peru Raises Rate for First Time in Almost 4 Years
body: Peru's Central Reserve Bank (BCRP) raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 4.50% in November 2026, its first increase in nearly four years, in line with market expectations. The decision reflected the impact of supply shocks, higher inflation expectations, and solid domestic demand. Annual inflation accelerated to 5.3% in October from 4.5% in September, driven mainly by rising food and energy costs. Core inflation excluding food and energy edged up to 4.6% from 4.5%, while the measure excluding food, energy, and transportation held at 2.0%, remaining within the central bank's 1%-3% target range. Twelve-month inflation expectations stayed at 3.1%, above the upper bound of the target. The BCRP expects inflation to gradually return to the target range and converge toward 2% as supply-side shocks recede, but cautioned that El Niño and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East could prolong price pressures. Economic activity indicators remained strong in October, and although business confidence eased, it stayed in optimistic territory. The central bank emphasized that this rate hike does not necessarily signal the start of a broader monetary tightening cycle. title: NZX 50 Retreats from Record High but Poised for 3rd Weekly Gain
body: The NZX 50 fell 80 points, or 0.6%, to 14,179 in Friday morning trade, following a weak lead from Wall Street overnight. Sentiment was hit by a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares after the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang, while rising oil prices pushed US Treasury yields higher. Profit-taking also weighed on the local market after the benchmark index notched a record high in the previous session, buoyed by strong earnings from several heavyweight stocks. Fresh domestic data further dampened risk appetite, showing that growth in New Zealand's manufacturing sector slowed in October amid higher fuel costs, elevated living expenses, and uncertainty surrounding the upcoming election. Climbing oil prices added to the pressure on equities by intensifying inflation worries and reinforcing expectations of further interest rate increases. Almost all sectors traded lower, led by industrials, with notable declines in Auckland International Airport (-3.4%), Turners Automotive (-1.9%), Fletcher Building (-1.6%), and Brisco Group (-1.2%). Despite the session's pullback, the NZX 50 was still up 1.3% for the week, recording its third consecutive weekly gain. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: South Korea Import Prices Rise in October

In contrast, capital goods prices declined 4.2%, and consumer goods prices fell 3.3%. By sector, mining product prices jumped 40.7%, propelled by a 47.6% surge in coal, crude petroleum, and natural gas prices. This reflected elevated international crude oil and gas prices stemming from supply disruptions related to the US–Iran war. Prices of manufactured goods increased 4.8%, largely due to a 52.5% rise in coal and petroleum products. Meanwhile, prices of agricultural, forestry, and marine products fell 1.9%, weighed down by an 8% decrease in livestock product prices. The Net Barter Terms of Trade Index rose 21.3%, while the Import Price Index edged down 1.8% compared with the previous month. title: Brazilian Real Extends Losses on Fiscal Concerns
body: The Brazilian real weakened beyond 5.65 per USD in November, extending its lowest level since May of last year, after the government's fiscal adjustment bill disappointed investors. While markets had initially welcomed the proposal as a first step toward a more robust fiscal agenda, they now see it as a modest and insufficient effort. Rather than tackling structural reforms needed to reverse the upward trajectory of public debt, the bill is viewed as mainly creating additional room for spending freezes to meet the 0.5% of GDP primary surplus target for 2027. The government has come under market pressure to deliver credible fiscal measures ever since Brazilian assets slumped following President Lula's reelection. At the same time, annual inflation rose to 4.63% in October from 4.58% in September, coming in below market expectations of 4.74% but still marking a four-month high and remaining above the central bank's 4.5% target ceiling. With inflation persisting above target, the Banco Central do Brasil is expected to proceed cautiously before resuming its Selic rate-cutting cycle. title: Brazil 10-Year Yield Rises as Fiscal Adjustment Bill Disappoints
body: The yield on Brazil's 10-year government bond climbed to around 15.37%, staying close to the ten-year peak of 15.75% reached on November 3, after the government's fiscal adjustment proposal disappointed investors. Initial market reaction to the fiscal package had been positive, as it was seen as a first step toward a more robust fiscal framework. However, sentiment has shifted, and the bill is now viewed as a modest and insufficient adjustment. Analysts note that the measures do not prioritize structural reforms capable of reversing the upward trajectory of public debt. Instead, they largely expand the scope for expenditure freezes in an effort to meet the government's primary surplus target of 0.5% of GDP by 2027. On the inflation front, annual consumer price growth accelerated to 4.63% in October from 4.58% in September, below market expectations of 4.74% but still a four‑month high and above the Central Bank of Brazil's 4.5% target ceiling. With inflation running above target, the BCB is expected to maintain a cautious stance and delay any resumption of its Selic rate‑cutting cycle. body: Crude oil climbed to about $89 a barrel on Thursday, extending gains for a second straight session and rebounding from a ten-week low of $86 hit on November 10th. Iran has shown little willingness to soften its stance. Notably, the USDA increased upcoming crop estimates for both Argentina and Brazil by 2 million metric tons each. Traders also look ahead to Friday's weekly USDA export sales report, delayed one day due to the Veterans Day holiday, following recent flash sales to Mexico.

Market participants are closely monitoring broader equity market volatility and its potential impact on consumer beef demand during the seasonal lull between peak grilling and holiday buying.
